lines.text:
Behind the Counter — How a Pharmacy Works

A pharmacy is more than a shop that sells medicine. It is a healthcare service staffed by trained professionals who prepare, check, and advise on medication. Understanding how a pharmacy works — and the vocabulary that goes with it — is useful for anyone who takes medicine or cares for someone who does.

The pharmacy counter is where patients hand in their prescription — a written order from a doctor listing the medication, dose, and instructions. The pharmacist reads the prescription, checks the patient profile on the computer for allergies or other medications, and prepares the order. A label printer produces a sticker with the patient's name, the drug name, the dose, and the instructions. A barcode scanner records the transaction at the cash register.

Medicine comes in many forms. A tablet is a small, solid pill that you swallow. A capsule is similar but has a soft outer shell filled with powder or liquid. A syrup is a liquid medicine, often flavoured for children. A cream or an ointment is applied to the skin. Eye drops go into the eyes. An inhaler delivers medicine directly into the lungs — essential for asthma patients. An injection delivers medicine through a needle. A patch sticks to the skin and releases medicine slowly. A lozenge dissolves in the mouth, often for sore throats. A nasal spray is sprayed into the nose. Ear drops go into the ears. A suppository is inserted into the body. An injection pen allows patients to inject themselves at home — common for diabetes.

Behind the counter, the pharmacist uses specialised tools. A digital scale weighs precise amounts. A mortar and pestle grinds tablets into powder for patients who cannot swallow pills. A pill counter sorts exact numbers of tablets. A pill cutter divides tablets into smaller doses. A pill organiser — a box with compartments for each day — helps patients remember their medicine. A refrigerator stores medicines that need to stay cold. A medicine shelf holds hundreds of different products, alphabetically arranged. A medicine cabinet in the dispensary keeps controlled substances secure.

The front of the pharmacy sells products that don't need a prescription. A bandage and a plaster treat small cuts. A thermometer checks body temperature. A blood pressure monitor reads blood pressure at home. A glucose meter measures blood sugar. A pregnancy test provides results in minutes. Hand sanitiser and disinfectant kill germs. Cotton balls and gauze are used for cleaning wounds. Vitamin supplements, mineral supplements, and herbal remedies fill an entire aisle.

The pharmacist wears a pharmacist coat — usually white — and is qualified to answer questions about side effects, drug interactions, dosage, and safe storage. They are often the first healthcare professional people speak to when they feel unwell.

A pharmacy runs on precision. The wrong dose, the wrong drug, or the wrong combination can be dangerous. Every label is checked twice. Every prescription is verified. In a pharmacy, accuracy is not just good practice — it is a matter of safety.

lines.text: 'Pharmacy' is universal. 'Chemist's' is British (Boots is the most famous chain). 'Drugstore' is American (CVS, Walgreens). American drugstores often sell snacks, drinks, and household items — more like a convenience store.
lines.name: 'Pharmacy' is universal. 'Chemist's' is British (Boots is the most famous chain). 'Drugstore' is American (CVS, Walgreens). American drugstores often sell snacks, drinks, and household items — more like a convenience store.

lines.text: In England, each prescription item costs a fixed charge (currently around £9.90). In Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland, prescriptions are free. Children under 16, over-60s, and people with certain conditions are exempt from charges.

lines.text: 'Medicine' is neutral — something you take to treat illness. 'Drug' can mean medicine (especially in American English) but also refers to illegal substances. In the UK, 'drugs' in everyday speech often implies illegal drugs, so 'medicine' or 'medication' is safer.

lines.text: 'GP' is the British term for a family doctor. You 'see your GP' or 'make an appointment with your GP'. The American equivalent is 'primary care physician' or 'family doctor'. 'Surgery' (BrE) = the GP's office: 'I called the surgery.'

lines.text: 'Medicine' is usually uncountable when referring to the substance: 'some medicine', 'take your medicine.' Use 'a medicine' only when distinguishing between types: 'This is a medicine for headaches.' 'Medication' (uncountable) is more formal: 'He takes medication daily.'

lines.text: 'Three times a day' — no 'in.' 'Once a week', 'twice a month', 'three times a year.' The article 'a' means 'per' or 'each.' 'She visits the pharmacy once a month.' Never 'in a day' for frequency — 'in a day' means 'within a single day': 'I finished it in a day.'

lines.text: 'Advice' is uncountable: 'some advice', 'a piece of advice.' Not: 'an advice' or 'advices.' The verb is 'advise' (different spelling, different pronunciation). 'I advise you to take vitamin D.' 'She gave me good advice.'

lines.text: 'A headache', 'a stomachache', 'a toothache', 'a backache' — these use 'a' because they are countable conditions. But: 'I have flu' (no article, BrE) or 'I have the flu' (AmE). Disease names: 'She has diabetes' (no article), 'He has a cold' (article).

lines.text: 'Suggest' never takes object + infinitive (*suggested me to take). Correct: 'suggested that I take' (subjunctive) or 'suggested taking' (-ing form). The same pattern applies to 'recommend': 'She recommended taking vitamin C.' Never 'recommended me to take.'
